finding: §2's safety argument rests on a false code claim. It states the severity field 'is already validated' and that 'audit_schema.go rejects a row that omits it', concluding 'Nothing new is asserted by the agent being measured' — the single sentence that separates severity from the thrice-deferred scope field. Measured: internal/cli/audit_schema.go contains one function, renderAuditOutputSchema, whose doc comment reads 'renders the NDJSON output schema block embedded in every audit prompt'. Its line 24 writes the string '- severity: field MUST exist; null for PASS, one of error|warning|info for PARTIAL or FAIL' into the prompt. It validates nothing. Confirmed a second way: the token 'severity' appears zero times in internal/cli/audit_record.go, and a sweep of every production .go file under internal/ returns 171 lines, none of which is an audit-side severity check — there is no ValidAuditSeverity, and engine.SeverityRank knows only critical|high|medium|low, ranking error/warning/info alike as unknown. The contrast is decisive because tp already paid for this exact mistake with the sibling field: category IS checked at the sink by invalidCategoryRows in audit_record.go, whose own comment says it exists because 'tp renders the enum into every auditor prompt through engine.RenderAuditCategoryText, in words that promise "unknown values are rejected" — and then never looked at what came back.' §2 reads a prompt-side MUST as a validator, which is that defect's definition. Consequence for the design, not just the citation: severity on a PARTIAL/FAIL row is a self-declared judgement written by the agent whose work is being gated, with nothing to check it against — which is verbatim v0.33.0 §5 Non-Goal 1's test for why scope may not gate ('role is an attribution the sub-agent copies from the prompt tp gave it, checkable against the panel tp emitted, while a scope label is a judgement with nothing to check it against'). severity falls on the scope side of that line, not the role side, so §2's central distinction does not hold as written.
suggestion: Either (a) drop 'already validated' and make the sink check part of this release — a row whose status is PARTIAL or FAIL and whose severity is outside error|warning|info is refused by tp audit --record, mirroring invalidCategoryRows line-for-line, with a §7 test that a hand-edited row carrying severity 'trivial' or null is rejected rather than counted clean; or (b) keep severity unvalidated and rewrite §2's third paragraph to argue the gate is safe for some other reason, since the 'nothing new is asserted' reason is unavailable. Do not ship the claim as it stands: it is the load-bearing sentence of the release.

finding: §4 falsifies §2.1's table and §7 test 4, in the same release, on this repository's own recorded data. §4 resets consecutive_clean to zero whenever tp audit --record sees a spec_hash different from the previous round's. §2.1 claims blocking converges v0.35.0 at round 3 and all at round 9, and §7 test 4 makes that replay the acceptance evidence that the change is 'opt-in rather than a silent reinterpretation'. Measured from spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/state.json, the nine audit rounds' spec hashes are r1 a46f45c6, r2 a46f45c6, r3 c06544ea, r4 50be1428, r5 2dd780c6, r6 6f42a8eb, r7 1259a4af, r8 1259a4af, r9 54e031e6 — the hash changes at r3, r4, r5, r6, r7 and r9, six of nine rounds. Under §4, r3's reset zeroes the streak blocking needed, so blocking does not converge at round 3; and r9's reset zeroes the streak r8 built, so all does not converge at round 9 either. Neither cell of the table survives the section three headings later, and 'all reproduces the recorded history exactly' — the sentence that carries the opt-in argument — is false once §4 ships, regardless of which value audit_converge_on takes. (v0.36.0 differs by luck: r2 and r3 share f7da0fde, so blocking's round-3 stop survives there.) A second, unstated cost falls out of the same measurement: the spec moved between rounds in 13 of the 22 recorded audit rounds across the two cycles, so in this repository §4's reset is the normal case, not the exception — while §7 test 8 pins only the case that does not occur ('a cycle whose spec never changes ... so the reset costs nothing when nothing moved').
suggestion: State the composition explicitly and re-derive the evidence under it. Concretely: (1) say in §2.1 whether the replay is computed with §4 active or with §4 held out, and if held out say why that is a fair test of a release that ships both; (2) re-run the table under both mechanisms and print the resulting cells, or withdraw the 'reproduces the recorded history exactly' claim; (3) add a §7 test for the case the data says is normal — a cycle whose spec moves between two otherwise-clean rounds — beside test 8's no-movement case; (4) fix the ordering for decomposition: test 4 as written is unwritable once §4 lands, so either it is written and run before §4's task, or it is restated over a fixture whose hash is held constant.

finding: The table is presented as a measurement 'in both directions' with v0.35.0 as 'the case for the release' and v0.36.0 as the only case against. Replayed row by row against the recorded rounds, both cycles are cases against the default, and the column that would show it is the one the table omits. Per-round non-PASS severity, computed from spec/.tp-review/*/state.json and the round files: v0.35.0 r1 {error 2, warning 5, info 5}, r2 {warning 5, info 7}, r3 {warning 2, info 3}, r4 {error 1, warning 2, info 1}, r5 {warning 6}, r6 {warning 1}, r7 {warning 1, info 1}, r8 {}, r9 {}. So blocking stops that cycle after r3 — and r4, the very next round, carries an error row. §2.1 discounts two of v0.36.0's three round-7 errors as 'repair artifacts of round 6 [that] would not exist in a cycle that had stopped at round 3'; that defence is unavailable for v0.35.0's r4 error, which is one round past the proposed stop, not four. The honest score of the spec's own instrument is therefore 2 of 2 cycles in which blocking would have shipped over an error-severity row, not 1 of 2. The framing hides it because the columns ask when the loop stops rather than what was still to be found after it stopped; a third column, 'highest severity recorded after the blocking stop', reads error for v0.35.0 (r4) and error for v0.36.0 (r7, r12, r13). §2.1's closing sentence — 'the two cycles disagree, and one sample each way is not a policy' — is the sentence this row falsifies: they do not disagree.
suggestion: Add the third column and recompute the reading. Then make the default an explicit, argued choice rather than a symmetry ('matching review_converge_on, so the asymmetry disappears'): either ship all as the default and let blocking be the opt-in, which is what 2-of-2 supports, or keep blocking and state plainly in §2 that both measured cycles would have shipped over an error row and name what makes that acceptable — §2.0a's 'ask the role whether it still holds its own prior reasoning' is a candidate but is currently cited as a caveat rather than as a condition on the default.

finding: The release turns on which audit severities block, and §2 never says. Its predicate reads 'blocking counts a round clean when no surviving non-PASS row carries a blocking severity' — a definition in terms of an undefined set. The set is recoverable only by inference, from §2.1's parentheticals ('r2, r3 carry zero error') and §7 tests 2 and 3, i.e. blocking = {error}. The review twin does not do this: v0.31.0 §4.1 states its set normatively ('The blocking severities are critical and high ... medium and low do not'), fixes it as not itself a knob, and — the half that matters more here — states the conservative rule for a severity that is missing or out of vocabulary: it is 'treated conservatively as blocking, so an ill-formed severity from an LLM reviewer never lets a genuine defect count toward convergence' (engine/reviewclean.go implements exactly that). §2 states neither, and the omission is reachable rather than theoretical: measured across this repository's v0.35.0 and v0.36.0 audit rounds, all 2913 PASS rows carry an explicit severity key whose value is JSON null, so null is a value the recorded corpus actually contains, nothing rejects it on a PARTIAL/FAIL row (see the §2 row above), and the spec does not say whether such a row blocks. Left unstated, the implementer's default — a map lookup that misses — fails OPEN, which is the direction v0.31.0 deliberately refused.
suggestion: Add a normative clause in §2 with three parts, mirroring v0.31.0 §4.1: (1) the blocking audit severity set is {error}, and it is fixed in this release rather than configurable; (2) matching is case-insensitive after trimming; (3) a non-PASS row whose severity is null, absent, or outside error|warning|info is treated conservatively as blocking. Then add a §7 test that pins part (3) specifically, since it is the one that decides whether the gate fails open.

finding: §5a's second change re-admits, under another name, the exact mechanism §2 and §6 Non-Goal 1 defer for a fourth time. '(2) A PASS carrying such a statement is an unresolved item for convergence, not a clean one' requires a new agent-written marker on a row whose presence blocks a release. §6 Non-Goal 1 defers scope because 'a self-declared label that gates a release is strictly worse than over-counting, because the agent whose work is being gated writes the label' — and that reason applies unchanged to a self-declared 'my prose knows something my verdict cannot carry' flag. §5a even supplies the aggravating detail: the note it proposes to gate on was, in its own fifth case, wrong on three of four files and had to be retracted by the same role a round later. Second, independent defect: the rule is inert under §2's own definitions. §2 fixes both predicates over non-PASS rows and defends that choice with a measurement ('every PASS row carries severity: null, so a predicate phrased over any row of any severity would read the wrong population'). A PASS row carrying a note is still a PASS row, so neither blocking nor all can see it. §5a therefore silently redefines the population §2 spent a paragraph fixing, and no section reconciles them. Under the conservative reading this review recommends elsewhere — a null severity is blocking — the reconciliation is worse, not better: every PASS-with-note row would block under blocking and not under all, inverting the two policies' strictness for that class of row.
suggestion: Pick one. Either (a) move §5a out of this release entirely — it is a finding-contract change, not a convergence-policy change, and §6 Non-Goal 5 already sends the neighbouring question ('a fourth row status') to spec/0.49.0.md §5, which is where this belongs beside it; or (b) keep it and pay its costs in full: name the new field, state in §2 that the convergence population is non-PASS rows plus PASS rows carrying that field, state how the field interacts with each of blocking and all so the strictness inversion cannot arise, answer Non-Goal 1's objection for this field specifically, and give it a §7 test. Recommendation: (a). §5a's first change — the brief asking each role to state what its row cannot carry — is cheap, non-gating, and can ship alone.

finding: §3 overturns two standing Non-Goals and a shipped guard test, and §6 records neither. spec/0.33.0.md §5 Non-Goal 5 reads 'Auto-resolving or parking a non-spec-coverage finding. tp has no audit-side --resolve. Adding one is how a round of open findings quietly becomes a clean round', and Non-Goal 8 reads 'Anything tp stores that then clears the gate is audit_converge_on under another name, and it would arrive without the policy debate item 2 defers.' §3's mechanism — a stored wontfix or duplicate disposition excluded from the round's finding count — is precisely 'something tp stores that then clears the gate'. The prohibition is not merely prose: internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go's TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate disposes a go-safety FAIL as wontfix, re-records, and asserts 'a wontfix disposition does not clear go-safety's open finding' and then that tp audit --status --check still exits 1, 'the gate is still shut over the disposed finding'. The same test asserts 'unknown workflow field: audit_converge_on', so §2 inverts it too. §3's own framing makes the omission easy to miss: it says the exclusion happens 'on the same terms review already excludes a resolved finding', but review's terms are not these — engine/reviewclean.go excludes a finding resolved wontfix/duplicate whatever its severity, while §3 must additionally distinguish fixed, and the stored object is {status, evidence, resolved_at} (internal/cli/audit_resolve.go's disposition()) rather than a field named 'disposition'. §3 names neither the field path nor the values it reads.
suggestion: Add an 'Overturns' paragraph to §6 or §3 naming, with citations, v0.31.0 §4.4/Non-Goal 4/test 8, v0.33.0 §5 Non-Goals 2, 5 and 8, and v0.34.0 §11 Non-Goal 2 — stating for each why the reason given then no longer holds. Add a §7 test asserting the inversion deliberately, so TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate's two assertions are changed by a task that owns them rather than by whoever hits them first. And in §3, name the exact read: row['resolved']['status'] ∈ {wontfix, duplicate} excluded, 'fixed' not excluded, absent 'resolved' not excluded.

finding: §2's account of why the knob was deferred three times does not match the record it cites, and it omits the one deferral that was about severity. (1) 'The two were bundled under one heading and only one of them was risky' — they were not bundled: spec/0.33.0.md §5 lists them as separate Non-Goals 1 and 2, and Non-Goal 2's reason is a dependency, not a shared risk: 'It has no meaning without item 1.' spec/0.34.0-candidates.md §2 restates the same dependency ('Without a trustworthy scope, the knob has nothing to select on'). (2) The deferred knob is not this knob. spec/0.33.0-candidates.md §1 designs audit_converge_on as 'spec | all, default spec' — a selector over the scope field. This release proposes 'blocking | all' over severity. Those are different fields sharing a name, so 'the same objection was aimed at both' is not the right description of what happened; the honest description is that the name is being reused for a different design, which is a stronger position and should be argued as such. (3) The omission that matters: §2 cites 0.33.0, 0.34.0 and 0.35.0 and never cites v0.31.0 — the release that shipped review_converge_on and explicitly declined to mirror it into audit, for a reason about severity rather than scope. spec/0.31.0.md §4.4: 'Audit convergence is unchanged ... its error | warning | info severity is a display annotation the stop check never reads ... This release adds no severity-awareness to audit convergence and no audit_converge_on field. Audit runs to two consecutive clean rounds as before; implementation correctness is not negotiable against severity.' Non-Goal 4 repeats it and test 8 pins 'there is no audit_converge_on'. §2's claim 'That objection does not touch severity' is true of v0.33.0's objection and false of v0.31.0's, which touches nothing else.
suggestion: Rewrite the paragraph around the real history: say that the deferred audit_converge_on was a scope selector and that this one is a severity selector sharing its name; drop 'bundled under one heading'; and add a paragraph quoting v0.31.0 §4.4's actual objection — 'implementation correctness is not negotiable against severity' — and answering it. That answer is the release's real argument and it is currently missing.

finding: §5b's proposed fix reverses a documented contract sentence that a guard test pins verbatim, and does not say so. §5b: 'a recorded round should carry forward the roles it did not receive, marked as not-run rather than dropped, so a streak can neither advance nor vanish on their behalf.' The shipped contract says the opposite: 'A role with no rows in a round is not clean in it, so its streak ends.' That sentence is required verbatim in skills/tp/REFERENCE.md by internal/cli/docs_contract_test.go's referenceSignalSentences list, which exists (per its own comment) so 'a release that ships the fields without the wording' fails. Carrying a role forward is exactly a streak that neither ends nor advances, so the sentence and the fix cannot both stand. There is a second reason to be careful here rather than to just flip it: the current rule fails toward more auditing, which spec/0.33.0.md §1 states as a standing constraint for everything in that design ('Every rule that could fail in two directions fails toward keep auditing'). Carrying a role forward fails the other way — a role that has not been run for five rounds keeps a streak it did not earn — and §5b's own argument is that a narrow round should not read as progress.
suggestion: Name the sentence and its guard in §5b, and state the replacement wording that REFERENCE.md must then carry. Then prefer the fail-toward-auditing shape over carry-forward: report the missing role explicitly (a not_run marker in role_streaks, and spec_coverage_clean_rounds unchanged rather than nulled when the role was simply not part of the round), while keeping the rule that a not-run role's streak does not advance. That answers §5b's actual complaint — a narrow round silently setting the ship-rule quantity to null — without granting a role credit it did not earn.

finding: §2.1's table gives v0.36.0 as '7 and open' recorded rounds. Measured from spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/state.json: 13 recorded audit rounds, files audit-round-1.ndjson through audit-round-13.ndjson, all present on disk. The same spec contradicts its own cell three times — §5's table tabulates rounds 10, 11, 12 and 13; §5b is measured 'against tp's own state at v0.36.0 audit round 12'; §2.0a cites 'v0.36.0's rounds 12 and 13'. The number is not decorative: it is the denominator of the row that carries the entire case against the default, and 'round 7, four rounds after blocking would have closed the phase' reads very differently when it is round 7 of 13 rather than the open edge of 7.
suggestion: Change the cell to '13 and open'. Then re-read the sentences that lean on it: with rounds 8-13 in view, v0.36.0 recorded error rows at r7, r12 and r13, so 'that cycle's round 7 ... recorded three error rows' understates its own case — r12 and r13 carry two error rows each, and §2.0a already treats those as the release's central caveat. Bind the count to the artifact rather than restating it, e.g. 'every audit-round-N.ndjson recorded under spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/'.

finding: §4 opens 'audit has no equivalent', and that is not accurate as stated. engine.Converged is `ConsecutiveClean(rounds) >= requiredCleanRounds && !StateStale(rounds, currentHash)`, and StateStale compares the spec on disk against the LAST RECORDED ROUND's spec_hash — so a spec amended after the last recorded round already blocks convergence today, on both review and audit, and divergence condition 3 reads the same flag. What audit genuinely lacks is only the between-rounds case: a spec amended, then a fresh round recorded against the new text, which restores !StateStale while the earlier rounds in the streak were read against different bytes. §4 should claim that narrower gap, because as written it invites an implementation that duplicates a guard tp already has. The section also introduces a third hash comparison without relating it to the two that exist — StateStale (disk vs latest round), RolesStale (current corpus vs latest round's stored roles_hash), and now §4's (this round vs previous round) — and states no precedence among them or what --status reports when two disagree. Finally, §4 removes an asymmetry a prior release states as deliberate: spec/0.33.0.md §1, 'The two staleness axes are deliberately not symmetric — a corpus change ends the streak, a spec change only has to be absent at the moment of reporting.' §4 makes the spec axis end the streak too, which may well be right, but it is an overturn and is not recorded as one.
suggestion: Narrow the opening claim to the between-rounds case and say what Converged/StateStale already covers. Name all three comparisons in one place with their precedence and their reported fields. Add a sentence overturning spec/0.33.0.md §1's asymmetry explicitly, with the reason it no longer holds. And state the boundary case §4 leaves open: what happens on the FIRST recorded round, where there is no previous round to differ from.

finding: Half the spec's normative sections have no test. Tests 1-4 cover §2, test 5 covers §3, tests 6-8 cover §4. §5, §5a and §5b — three sections that between them change what --check measures, what makes a round clean, and how a round's roles are recorded — carry none. §5 is the sharpest case because it does state its test, in prose, and that test never reaches §7: 'the test is the one v0.36.0 would have failed: a fixture where the conformance role is clean for required_clean_rounds running while another role has open non-FAIL rows must reach exit 0, and must not reach it if the conformance role has an open row.' A test stated in a body section and absent from the Tests section will not be decomposed: tasks take source_sections, and the section that owns the behaviour is not the section a test task would be pointed at.
suggestion: Either promote the prose tests into §7 — §5's exit-0/exit-1 fixture pair, §5a's 'none of the four rounds named above was clean' as a replayable assertion, §5b's one-role round preserving rather than nulling the counter — or move §5, §5a and §5b out of this release. Leaving them normative-but-untested is the option to avoid: it is what lets an implementer close the release with §2, §3 and §4 done and three sections silently unimplemented.

finding: §5 is headed 'What this release must decide' and then declines to decide: 'The candidate shapes, neither chosen here.' The two candidates are not variants of one design — the first adds a new workflow field (converge_roles) with its own resolution precedence, validation, config --resolved surface and staleness interaction; the second changes the meaning of an existing exit code on --status --check and demotes the all-roles count to advisory, which is a contract change to an output every CI wired to tp reads. They differ in surface, in blast radius, and in which of §6's Non-Goals they brush against. A section in this state cannot be decomposed into tasks with acceptance, and the release cannot state its own exit-code contract.
suggestion: Choose before decomposition, and say which on the evidence: the exit-code reinterpretation is the smaller change but silently alters what an existing green CI means, while converge_roles is additive and leaves today's --check meaning intact for anyone who does not set it. If the choice cannot be made in this cycle, make §5 a Non-Goal pointing at the release that decides it, and keep §2/§3/§4 — that is a coherent release on its own. What must not happen is decomposition starting with §5 unresolved, because §5's shape decides whether §2's audit_converge_on is read by --check at all.

finding: §5's first candidate is 'a role-scoped convergence set (converge_roles, defaulting to the conformance role)', and 'the conformance role' is not a general tp concept — it is a hardcoded id. engine/rolestreaks.go: `const RoleSpecCoverage = "spec-coverage"`, with the comment 'the only role in the corpus that measures spec conformance', and engine.SpecCoverageCleanRounds returns nil unless a streak entry's Role equals that literal byte-for-byte. Auditor corpora are user-defined (.tp/auditors/*.json) and, since v0.32.0, per-spec deactivatable; tp's own corpus contains spec-coverage only because tp chose to name it that. So in a project whose corpus has no role with that exact id — or a spec that deactivates it — spec_coverage_clean_rounds is permanently null, and a --check defaulting to 'the conformance role' has no quantity to read. §5 states no rule for that state, which means the release's own gate would fail open or shut with nothing in the spec deciding which. §5b's transcript shows the same null arriving from a different direction, so this is not a hypothetical corner.
suggestion: State the absent-role rule normatively in §5: when converge_roles resolves to a set no role in the active corpus satisfies, --check must refuse rather than pass (fail toward keep-auditing, per spec/0.33.0.md §1's standing constraint) and must say which configured role ids were not found. Better still, key the default off the corpus rather than a literal — the role carrying the spec-derived checklist — and if that is not derivable today, say so and keep the literal with the refusal rule attached.

finding: §5 and §5b have a hard ordering dependency that neither states. §5 proposes moving --check onto the conformance role's streak; §5b measures that the same quantity is silently set to null by a round recorded with one role, reports it as clean:true, and notes this is newly easy — 'v0.36.0 shipped --role, which makes a one-role round easy to run for the first time, and the interactive fallback runs exactly one role per unit.' If §5 lands first, the release moves the release gate onto a counter it has, in the adjacent section, just documented as erasable by the workflow this repository actually runs. §6 and §7 state no ordering, and §7 has no test for either section, so nothing in the spec prevents the tasks being scheduled in that order.
suggestion: State in §5 that §5b is a prerequisite: --check may not be re-based on the conformance streak until a round that did not receive a role can no longer null it. If only one of the two can ship this cycle, ship §5b — it is a defect with a measured reproduction, while §5 is still choosing a mechanism.

finding: §5a's first change — 'The brief asks each role to state anything its prose knows that its row cannot carry, and to say what should be done about it' — is a change to the emitted audit prompt, and it lands on structures the suite pins verbatim. internal/cli/docs_contract_test.go pins two prompt orders as required substrings: specCoverageOrder = 'Role → Role Rules → Spec Excerpt → JSON-array Checklist → Affected Files → Output Schema' and sharedArmOrder = 'Role → Role Rules → Project Context → JSON-array Checklist → Disposition → Affected Files → Output Schema'. Neither has a slot for a new block. The arm that matters is the one with less room: internal/cli/audit_roles.go renders the Disposition block only `if role != roleSpecCoverage`, so spec-coverage's prompt has no precedent for a block between the checklist and the affected files — and every one of §5a's five measured cases is a spec-coverage row. So the new clause must reach the arm the existing per-arm split excludes, and §5a says only 'the brief' without naming the position, the arm, or the documents that carry the order.
suggestion: Name the position in both orders and update both pinned strings in the same task, or attach the clause to the Output Schema block (which both arms already render) rather than adding a seventh section. Either way say explicitly that the clause reaches spec-coverage, since that is the arm the section's own evidence comes from and the arm the current per-role split would skip by default.

finding: §1 closes 'This release gives audit the two things review already has: a severity-aware convergence policy, and a reason to distrust a streak that spans a changed spec.' The body ships at least five distinct mechanisms: audit_converge_on (§2), disposition-based exclusion from the finding count (§3), the spec-change streak reset (§4), a change to what --status --check measures (§5), a new gating marker on PASS rows plus a prompt change (§5a), and a change to how a round records roles it did not receive (§5b). The a/b suffixes make §5a and §5b read as facets of §5, but their subjects are three different things — which rows the gate reads, what a row can carry, and which roles a round contributes — with no shared fix and no shared test. This is worth raising as a structural finding rather than an editorial one because this repository has measured the cost: CLAUDE.md records spec length as the strongest single predictor of cycle length across fifteen cycles (r ≈ +0.56; under 200 lines ≈ 8-9 rounds, over 300 ≈ 23), and the release-splitting rule it derived — 'if a piece can be released independently, it is its own release'. At 288 lines with three sections still lacking a mechanism or a test, this spec is already on the expensive side of that line and will grow when they are supplied.
suggestion: Split. §2 + §3 + §4 is a coherent, independently releasable ~150-line spec: one policy field, one counting rule, one reset, eight tests, all three with mechanisms today. §5 + §5a + §5b is a second release about what quantity the gate should read and what a round records — and it is not ready, since §5 has no chosen mechanism, §5a needs a finding-contract change §6 Non-Goal 5 already routes elsewhere, and §5b reverses a pinned contract sentence. If the split is refused, at minimum rewrite §1's closing sentence to enumerate what actually ships, and renumber §5a/§5b as §6/§7 so the suffixes stop implying they are one topic.

finding: 'v0.36.0's rounds 12 and 13 produced two error-severity findings.' Counted from the recorded rounds: audit-round-12.ndjson carries 2 non-PASS rows, both severity error; audit-round-13.ndjson carries 3, of which 2 are error. That is four error rows across the two rounds, not two. The claim may be counting distinct defects rather than rows, which would be the more useful number, but the sentence does not say which and the two readings differ by a factor of two in a sentence the section calls 'one caveat this release must carry'. CLAUDE.md names this class directly — never assert a quantifier you did not count; bind the claim to an artifact or let a guard enforce it.
suggestion: State both numbers and their basis: 'four error-severity rows, two distinct defects (guards certifying a CI step that never runs), across audit-round-12.ndjson and audit-round-13.ndjson'. The row count is derivable from the files, so it cannot rot; the defect count is a judgement and should be labelled as one.

finding: 'engine/reviewconvergeon.go is twenty-four lines'. Verified correct today — the file is exactly 24 lines, two constants, a hint string and ValidReviewConvergeOn. Raising it anyway because it is a measured constant in prose with nothing binding it, the class CLAUDE.md records as going stale faster than a release, and because the number does no work: the argument is that the twin is small and shared, which the following clause already says. Recommendation, stated plainly rather than left as an observation: LEAVE the sentence, DROP the number. Rewrite to 'engine/reviewconvergeon.go is two constants, a hint string, and a predicate shared by the setter and every consumer.' That keeps the whole force of the point and removes the only part of it that can become false. Do not replace the number with a command that re-derives it — CLAUDE.md records that an under-specified recipe is worse than a stale number, because it can appear to confirm the opposite of what it defends.
suggestion: Delete 'is twenty-four lines:' and keep the enumeration that follows it.
